abstract: The light-driven water-splitting reaction of photosystem II exposes its key reaction center core protein subunits to irreversible oxidative photodamage. A rapid repair cycle replaces the photodamaged core subunits in plants, but how the large antenna–core supercomplex structures of plant photosystem II disassemble for repair is not currently understood. Here, we report the specific involvement of phosphorylation in removal of the peripheral antenna from the core and monomerization of the dimeric cores. However, monomeric cores disassemble further into smaller subcomplexes, even in the absence of phosphorylation, suggesting that there are other unknown mechanisms of disassembly. In this regard, we show that oxidative modifications of amino acids in core protein subunits of photosystem II are active mediators of monomeric core disassembly. Oxidative modifications thus likely disassemble only the damaged monomeric cores, ensuring an economical photosystem disassembly process. Taken together, our results suggest that phosphorylation and oxidative modification play distinct roles in photosystem II disassembly and repair.

Introduction
Oxygenic photosynthesis harnesses the potential of two nearly inexhaustible raw materials: sunlight and water, producing readily usable chemical energy in the form of ATP and NADPH. Central to oxygenic photosynthesis is the ability of photosystem II (PSII) to extract electrons and protons from abundant water through a light-driven redox reaction. The electrons derived from water are used by PSII to reduce the membrane-intrinsic electron carrier plastoquinone (PQ) to plastoquinol (PQH
2
), and the protons contribute to the proton motive force that drives ATP synthesis. Molecular oxygen, a byproduct of water oxidation, acts as a terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration to eventually release the chemical energy contained in photosynthates. A Mn
4
CaO
5
catalytic cluster is key to the remarkable water-splitting chemistry of PSII. However, in the absence of electron sinks and sources, as under intense sunlight or abiotic stresses, incomplete water oxidation and charge recombination events in PSII produce highly reactive hydrogen peroxide (H
2
O
2
), hydroxyl radical (HO
⋅
), and superoxide anion (O
2
⋅−
) (
Davis et al., 2016
;
Kale et al., 2017
). HO
⋅
and O
2
⋅−
oxidatively modify a number of key amino acid residues in the D1 and D2 reaction center proteins, impairing PSII function and causing photoinhibition, i.e., the light-induced loss of photosynthetic activity (
Mattoo et al., 1981
,
1984
;
Kyle et al., 1984
;
Aro et al., 1993
;
Kale et al., 2017
). Early irreversible oxidative modifications of amino acid ligands of the Mn
4
CaO
5
cluster and the non-heme iron trigger a cascade of additional modifications in D1 and D2, consistent with photoinhibition arising from photooxidative damage at both the donor and acceptor sides of PSII (
Kale et al., 2017
).
A robust repair process replaces the photodamaged D1 reaction center protein with a newly synthesized copy through an intricate cycle of disassembly of the holocomplex, degradation of the damaged D1,
de novo
synthesis and insertion of a nascent D1, and reassembly of the holocomplex (
Melis, 1999
;
Järvi et al., 2015
;
Johnson and Pakrasi, 2022
;
Komenda et al., 2024
). In plants, the repair of photodamaged D1 protein presents two major challenges (
Kirchhoff, 2013
). One is the disassembly of the large 1.4-MDa supercomplex of PSII formed by the light harvesting complex II (LHCII) peripheral antenna around a dimeric reaction center core (
Su et al., 2017
;
Cao et al., 2018
). The monomeric plant reaction center core comprises 20 protein subunits, with the D1 protein found buried at the core of the complex (
Wei et al., 2016
;
Cao et al., 2018
). The second challenge for repair of plant PSII is mobilization of the photodamaged supercomplexes from the tightly stacked granal thylakoid regions to the unstacked stroma lamellae for degradation of the photodamaged D1 and subsequent co-translational insertion of the nascent D1. Disassembly of the holocomplex may solve both of these problems, as disassembled smaller complexes are presumably more mobile (
Goral et al., 2010
;
Herbstova et al., 2012
). Although many aspects of the plant PSII repair cycle are well understood, little is known about the mechanism of PSII disassembly.
Two serine/threonine protein kinases, State Transition 7 (STN7) and 8 (STN8), phosphorylate PSII in a manner dependent on light quality and quantity (
Depege et al., 2003
;
Bellafiore et al., 2005
;
Bonardi et al., 2005
;
Rochaix, 2007
;
Pesaresi et al., 2011
). Although these two kinases act with some redundancy, STN7 predominately phosphorylates the peripheral trimeric LHCII protein in the acclimatory response of state transitions, whereas the major targets of STN8 are the PSII core protein subunits (
Depege et al., 2003
;
Bellafiore et al., 2005
;
Bonardi et al., 2005
;
Vainonen et al., 2005
). PSII phosphorylation is reversible, as a PSII Core Phosphatase (PBCP) dephosphorylates core phosphoproteins while a separate phosphatase targets the phospho-LHCII (
Pribil et al., 2010
;
Shapiguzov et al., 2010
;
Samol et al., 2012
). Over the years, core protein phosphorylation has been suggested to somehow facilitate the PSII repair cycle (
Puthiyaveetil and Kirchhoff, 2013
). However, analysis of a knockout mutant of STN8, with significantly reduced core phosphorylation, and a double mutant of STN7 and STN8, which lacked PSII phosphorylation altogether, surprisingly revealed little effect on D1 turnover (
Bonardi et al., 2005
). The PSII function of the mutant plants was nevertheless slightly affected in high light. Two follow-up studies, however, reported slower D1 turnover in the
stn8
mutant (
Tikkanen et al., 2008
;
Fristedt et al., 2009
). Tikkanen et al. also found high light sensitivity of PSII, increased oxidative damage to thylakoid proteins, and decreased disassembly of PSII in the mutant. Subsequent analyses have also suggested a role for phosphorylation in PSII disassembly, but exactly how phosphorylation promotes disassembly remains unclear. Offering a potential mechanism, a structural map of PSII core phosphorylation showed the strategic location of phosphosites at the peripheral antenna attachment sites and at the monomer–monomer interface (
Puthiyaveetil and Kirchhoff, 2013
). This placement is consistent with a role for phosphorylation in peripheral antenna dissociation and core monomerization. However, the specific predictions of this phosphorylation map have not yet been tested. Using biochemical, biophysical, and mass spectrometry approaches in the model plant
Arabidopsis thaliana
, we reexamined the role of core phosphorylation in PSII disassembly. We further tested whether photodamage, in the form of oxidative protein modification, has any role in promoting the disassembly of damaged PSII.
Results
Phosphorylation drives peripheral antenna dissociation and core monomerization
To probe the role of phosphorylation in PSII disassembly, we first undertook a mass spectrometry (MS)-based analysis of wild type (Col-0) thylakoid samples using a phosphopeptide enrichment strategy. Our analysis confirmed many of the previously known PSII phosphoproteins and phosphosites (
Supplemental Table 1
). However, we also found some novel PSII core phosphoproteins: PsbL, PsbF, PsbQ-2, and PsbR.
Figure 1
A shows a superimposition of these phosphosites onto a pea PSII supercomplex structure. The two known phosphosites of PsbH and the newly identified PsbL phosphosite lie at the monomer–monomer interface, which is suggestive of their role in monomerization of the dimeric core. The known D1, D2, and CP43 phosphosites and the newly identified PsbF phosphosite are situated at the peripheral antenna attachment sites on the core, which is indicative of their possible role in peripheral antenna dissociation.
Figure 1
Protein phosphorylation as a driver of PSII disassembly.
(A)
A projection of known phosphosites onto a plant C2S2M2 supercomplex. Phosphoproteins are rendered in different colors (D1, green; D2, yellow; CP43, pink; PsbH, blue; PsbL, gray; and PsbF, red) and labeled. The D1 and CP43 phosphosites are predicted to drive the dissociation of the S-trimer from the core, and the D2 and PsbF phosphosites are predicted to drive that of the M-trimer. The two phosphosites of PsbH and a phosphosite of PsbL occur at the monomer–monomer interface and may therefore contribute to the monomerization of the dimeric reaction center cores. The phosphosite on the lumenal PsbQ-2 subunit is not shown in the current view, and neither is the PsbR phosphoprotein, owing to its uncertain location. The supercomplex is based on the pea PSII structure 5XNM.pdb (
Su et al., 2017
).
(B)

The amido black staining of the corresponding PVDF membrane is shown below the blot as a loading control, with the LHCII protein band labeled.
(C)

v
) is plotted against time for wild type and mutant thylakoid samples. Each fluorescence trace is the average of three biological replicates, with each biological replicate measured in technical triplicate.

reduction (kQ

We subsequently determined the core phosphorylation level in wild type
A. thaliana
(Col-0), a double knockout mutant of STN7 and STN8 (
stn7stn8
), a knockout mutant of STN8 (
stn8-1
), and an overexpressor of STN8 (
STN8oe
) under growth light (∼150 μmol m
−2
s
−1
).
Figure 1
B shows a phosphothreonine immunoblot of thylakoid samples from these plants. Under growth light,
stn7stn8
shows no core or LHCII phosphorylation, consistent with STN kinases being the sole drivers of PSII phosphorylation (
Rochaix, 2007
).
stn8-1
shows significantly reduced PSII core phosphorylation and slightly lower LHCII phosphorylation, in line with earlier observations of STN8’s major kinase activity toward PSII core proteins and a minor but physiologically relevant phosphorylation of LHCII (
Bonardi et al., 2005
;
Vainonen et al., 2005
;
Longoni et al., 2019
). The residual core phosphorylation in
stn8-1
(
Figure 1
B) is likely to be the result of STN7 activity, given the slight substrate overlap and redundancy between these two PSII kinases (
Rochaix, 2007
;
Pesaresi et al., 2011
).
STN8oe
had hyperphosphorylated cores as expected (
Wunder et al., 2013
) (
Figure 1
B).
After determining the basal PSII phosphorylation level of all genotypes under growth light (
Figure 1
B), we analyzed PSII antenna size by chlorophyll fluorescence induction (
Figure 1
C). Room temperature chlorophyll fluorescence arises from chlorophyll
a
molecules associated with PSII antenna. The rise in fluorescence from a minimal (F
o
) to a maximal (F
m
) value in the presence of the electron transport inhibitor 3-(3,4-dichlorophenyl)-1,1-dimethylurea (DCMU) indicates the progressive reduction of the primary quinone electron acceptor Q
A
. Under uniform illumination by a green actinic light, a faster rise in chlorophyll fluorescence indicates better excitonic connectivity between PSII units owing to a larger peripheral antenna (
Rappaport et al., 2007
).
Figure 1
C shows normalized chlorophyll fluorescence induction of isolated thylakoid samples. It is apparent that
STN8oe
had a smaller PSII antenna size, consistent with its hyperphosphorylated cores causing antenna disassembly. The other mutants, by contrast, showed no significant changes in chlorophyll fluorescence induction under growth light (
Figure 1
C).
Figure 1
D shows the rate constant of Q
A
reduction (kQ
A
−
), which is the inverse of the time required to reach 60% of the fluorescence rise (
Rappaport et al., 2007
). With its smaller and less connected peripheral antenna,
STN8oe
had the highest kQ
A
−
value, whereas other mutants showed no statistically significant differences from the wild type (
Figure 1
D).
To account for the possibility that chlorophyll fluorescence induction analysis is not sufficiently sensitive to detect subtle changes in PSII functional assembly, we analyzed the abundance of various PSII disassembly intermediates by blue native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (BN–PAGE). Thylakoid membranes were first isolated from plants grown under growth light, and the thylakoid protein complexes were solubilized with the mild detergent n-dodecyl α-D-maltoside (α-DM, Anatrace). The solubilized protein complexes were then resolved on a non-denaturing blue native gel. For PSII, at least four structural species can be discerned on the gel (
Figure 1
E) (
Pietrzykowska et al., 2014
;
Suorsa et al., 2015
). The largest structural species comprises a group of antenna–core supercomplexes, migrating as multiple bands on the top of the gel. The most intense band is a PSII supercomplex known as C2S2M2, consisting of a dimeric reaction center core (C2), two strongly bound trimeric LHCIIs (S2), and two moderately bound trimeric LHCIIs (M2). The strongly bound trimers (S-trimers) are tethered to the core through the monomeric LHCII protein CP26, and the moderately bound trimers (M-trimers) associate with the core via monomeric CP29 and CP24 LHCII proteins. C2S2M2 is the predominant assembly form of plant PSII under low-light conditions (
Kouřil et al., 2013
). A dimer of C2S2M2 migrates above the C2S2M2 band, and the bands below C2S2M2 correspond to smaller PSII antenna–core supercomplexes with a decreasing complement of the peripheral antenna (
Pietrzykowska et al., 2014
;
Suorsa et al., 2015
). The other three structural species of PSII are a dimeric core, a monomeric core, and the sub-monomeric complex Reaction Center 47 (RC47). RC47 contains D1, D2, and CP47 core subunits but lacks the CP43 intrinsic antenna protein (
Nickelsen and Rengstl, 2013
;
Järvi et al., 2015
;
Krynická et al., 2015
). Other thylakoid protein complexes, such as PSI and cytochrome
b
6
f
(cyt
b
6
f
), comigrate with some of the PSII structural species in the gel, and multimeric and trimeric LHCII complexes are also resolved (
Figure 1
E).

and
stn8-1

Figure 1

Figure 1

STN8oe

;
Tikkanen and Aro, 2012

−2
s
−1
white light for 2 h. These moderate light-treated plants showed lower LHCII phosphorylation and STN7-dependent core phosphorylation, as expected from inhibition of STN7 kinase activity at higher light intensities (
Supplemental Figure 1A
) (
Rintamaki et al., 2000
). STN8-mediated core phosphorylation persisted under high light, with

Supplemental Figure 1B

methods

Discussion
Since its first demonstration nearly four decades ago, the functional implication of PSII phosphorylation has been eagerly sought (
Bennett, 1977
). Phosphorylation of the peripheral antenna proteins has generally been referred to as antenna or LHCII phosphorylation and phosphorylation of the core protein subunits D1, D2, CP43, and PsbH broadly as core phosphorylation. Phosphorylation of LHCII is now firmly established as the basis of plant state transitions (
Allen et al., 1981
;
Rochaix, 2007
;
Pesaresi et al., 2011
). However, the precise function of core phosphorylation has remained elusive. Various roles have been proposed over the years, but the suggestion of an involvement in disassembly is supported by several recent studies (
Tikkanen et al., 2008
;
Fristedt and Vener, 2011
;
Puthiyaveetil and Kirchhoff, 2013
). Exactly how phosphorylation leads to PSII disassembly has, however, remained unclear. Our phosphorylation map of PSII (
Figure 1
A) predicts a role for core phosphorylation in peripheral antenna dissociation. Our observations of the overaccumulation of PSII antenna–core supercomplexes in kinase knockout mutants and underaccumulation in
STN8oe
(
Figures 1
E and 2) bear out this prediction and confirm earlier findings from other laboratories (
Tikkanen et al., 2008
;
Wunder et al., 2013
). The increased monomerization of the dimeric cores in
STN8oe
(
Figures 1
E and
2
) is also in line with an earlier study of STN8 (
Wunder et al., 2013
) and supports the suggestion that core phosphorylation leads to monomerization of the dimeric cores. The slower reduction of Q
A
in
STN8oe
and the induction of PSII disassembly in
in vitro
-phosphorylated thylakoids (
Figures 1
D and
3
) provide further evidence for the role of core phosphorylation as a modulator of PSII functional assembly. The newly observed phosphorylation of PsbL (
Supplemental Table 1
) and the location of this phosphosite at the monomer–monomer interface (
Figure 1
A) are especially interesting given the role of PsbL in dimerization of the core (
Suorsa et al., 2004
). PsbL phosphorylation may thus drive core monomerization in concert with the two known PsbH phosphosites (
Figure 1
A). Because D2 and PsbF phosphosites occur near the putative docking site of PsbS (
Figure 1
A) (
Su et al., 2017
), phosphorylation may prevent reattachment of PsbS and the M-trimer to the core. The function of PsbQ-2 and PsbR phosphorylation is unclear. PsbQ-2 is one of two isoforms of the lumenal PsbQ subunit of the PSII oxygen evolving complex (OEC) (
Yi et al., 2006
). PsbR is a transmembrane protein that interacts with the OEC protein PsbP (
Ljungberg et al., 1984
;
Ido et al., 2014
) and is required for OEC assembly (
Suorsa et al., 2006
). An intriguing possibility is that phosphorylation of PsbQ-2 and PsbR regulates the assembly of OEC. Indeed, the disassembly/reassembly of OEC is a poorly understood aspect of the PSII repair cycle (
Järvi et al., 2015
;
Komenda et al., 2024
). Core phosphorylation may thus facilitate PSII repair by promoting disassembly of the holocomplex. However, it should be noted that the level of core phosphorylation may not strictly correlate with the rate of repair under all conditions. Core phosphorylation-mediated peripheral antenna dissociation, for example, may simply abate PSII excitation pressure without the need for D1 repair.
The dephosphorylation of PSII core phosphoproteins by PBCP is likely to be a key event in the PSII repair cycle, as the efficient degradation of photodamaged D1 by its proteases requires prior D1 dephosphorylation (
Rintamaki et al., 1996
). Dephosphorylation may similarly be necessary for the reassembly of repaired reaction center cores into PSII supercomplexes given our (
Figures 1
,
2
, and
3
) and others’ demonstration that core phosphorylation leads to disassembly (
Tikkanen et al., 2008
;
Fristedt and Vener, 2011
). An implication of the latter is that phosphorylation will prevent reassembly if phosphorylated cores are not swiftly acted on by PBCP. The glutathione-mediated inhibition of PBCP in high light is consistent with this dual role of phosphorylation in initiating disassembly as well as preventing reassembly of disassembled complexes (
Liu et al., 2019
). The phosphorylated status of RC47 and CP43-precomplex (
Figure 3
E) supports this notion. A phosphorylation-driven pause in reassembly may thus ensure a temporal uncoupling of damage and repair so that only repaired monomeric cores reassemble with the peripheral antenna. This delay in repair and reassembly under photoinhibitory conditions may also prevent continued damage, given the smaller antenna cross section of the reaction center cores and the quenched nature of the detached peripheral antenna (
Betterle et al., 2009
).
Our analysis of PSII disassembly in kinase mutants and in
in vitro
-phosphorylated thylakoid samples (
Figures 1
,
2
,and
3
) makes it abundantly clear that phosphorylation accounts for only some disassembly steps and that other light-dependent mechanisms should be sought to fully explain PSII disassembly. Here, we provide compelling evidence for protein oxidative modification as a phosphorylation-independent mechanism for PSII core disassembly (
Figures 4
,
5
and
6
), which is currently one of the least understood facets of the repair cycle (
Komenda et al., 2024
). In our
in vitro
experiments, we used a range of peroxide concentrations because of the uncertainty of the H
2
O
2
concentration experienced
in vivo
. Depending on the environmental conditions, plastid peroxide concentrations could vary greatly
in vivo
. For example, profuse production of H
2
O
2
occurs in high light (
Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017
). With peroxide concentrations greater than 20 mM, we intended only to demonstrate a dose-dependent tendency in the C1 disassembly response. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that peroxide treatment of isolated reaction center cores (
Figure 4
C) leads to some non-native oxidative modifications owing to altered access of amino acid residues that are otherwise shielded or buried in the holocomplex. Nevertheless, the following observations underscore the physiological relevance of the C1 disassembly observed under exogenous peroxide treatment (
Figure 4
). (1) RC47 is the same stably accumulating PSII disassembly species under both exogenous peroxide treatment and growth light (
Figures 4
and
5
A). (2) An electron transport inhibitor that minimizes ROS production at the acceptor side of PSII causes less core disassembly (
Figure 5
A). (3) Many oxidative modifications enriched under peroxide treatment were the same as those observed in growth light (
Figure 6
C and 6D;
Supplemental Table 2
). As reported by others, PSII core subunits other than D1 are also oxidatively modified under growth light and high light (
Figure 6
and
Supplemental Table 2
) (
Dreaden et al., 2011
;
Kale et al., 2017
). Whether this warrants their degradation and replacement
in vivo
is unknown. The light-induced turnover of non-D1 subunits remains rather obscure.
Oxidative modification seems especially important for dissociation of the monomeric cores into sub-monomeric complexes (
Figures 4
and
5
), but it is not yet clear whether phosphorylation acts alone or synergistically with photooxidative damage for the disassembly of the peripheral antenna from the core and in core monomerization. The exogenous peroxide-driven disassembly of the
stn7stn8
reaction center core was especially striking (
Figure 4
C), offering insights into a solely damage-mediated PSII disassembly mechanism in the kinase double mutant. In the absence of phosphorylation, how might the mutant be able to dissociate its peripheral antenna and monomerize its dimeric reaction center core? It is possible that the oxidative damage-mediated breakup of its reaction center core (
Figure 4
C and 4D) has a greater destabilizing effect on its dimeric reaction center core and peripheral antenna. The direct conversion of PSII supercomplexes into RC47 at high exogenous peroxide concentrations supports a purely damage-mediated disassembly of PSII (
Supplemental Figure 4
). The novel disassembly intermediates C1–RC47 and RC47–RC47 were observed in isolated cores from
stn7stn8
as well as isolated thylakoids from wild type plants grown under normal growth light (
Supplemental Figures 4
and
6–8
). A nonphotochemical quenching (NPQ)-mediated detachment and aggregation of the M-trimer may yet represent an additional phosphorylation-independent disassembly mechanism for the peripheral antenna in both the wild type and the double mutant (
Betterle et al., 2009
).
A projection of oxidative protein modifications onto C1 and RC47 structures (
Figure 6
E and 6F;
Supplemental Figure 11
) shows an enrichment of modified amino acids in the vicinity of the Mn cluster and the non-heme iron, which is pertinent to the localized nature of the origin and spread of ROS from these two cofactors in PSII (
Kale et al., 2017
). Some of the RC47-exclusive oxidative modifications of D1 are clustered at the interface between the D1 and CP43 subunits, especially at the acceptor side of PSII (
Figure 6
G). The acceptor-side modifications of D1 at amino acid residues M139, R140, P141, and W142 are especially notable given their proximity to the C-terminal CP43 loop with which CP43 interlocks with D1 (
Figure 6
G and
Supplemental Table 2
). Oxidative modification of amino acid residues at this interface may thus weaken the D1–CP43 interaction, allowing dissociation of the monomeric cores along these subunits. Because we do not have any information on oxidative modification of the CP43 subunit (as part of the detached CP43-precomplex), it would be premature to conclude that damage-mediated disassembly of C1 is driven entirely by D1 modifications. Indeed, oxidative modification of CP43 (W352 in cyanobacteria and W365 in spinach) has been suggested as a trigger/signal for D1 replacement (
Anderson et al., 2002
;
Dreaden et al., 2011
). Our
Arabidopsis
CP43 data include this modification (
Supplemental Table 2
). The novelty of our observation, however, is that we demonstrate oxidative modification of core proteins as a disassembly mechanism for removal of the CP43-precomplex from the monomeric core, thereby exposing the damaged D1 to proteases. A role for ROS species in selective cleavage of the D1 protein has been noted previously (
Miyao et al., 1995
). This may represent yet another damage-mediated disassembly mechanism for the PSII monomeric core. A Trp oxidation at the D1 N terminus helps the FtsH protease to recognize and selectively degrade the damaged D1 (
Kato et al., 2023
). By these mechanisms, oxidative modifications may ensure the specific disassembly and degradation of only the damaged monomeric cores, sparing undamaged monomeric cores for swift reassembly into PSII supercomplexes (
Figure 7
). Oxidative protein modification may be especially significant for the disassembly and repair of PSII in organisms such as cyanobacteria and nongreen algae that lack PSII phosphorylation altogether (
Johnson and Pakrasi, 2022
). Oxidative protein modification is also likely to be the ancient disassembly mechanism of PSII, and core-protein phosphorylation may have originated later in evolution to enable explicit control over the disassembly and repair processes of plant and green algal PSII.

Methods
Plant materials, growth conditions, and isolation of thylakoid membranes
A. thaliana
(Col-0) wild type,
stn8-1
,
stn7stn8
, and
STN8oe
plants were grown from seeds on soil at 21°C under a white growth light of ∼150 μmol m
−2
s
−1
under an 8-h light/16-h dark short-day photoperiod. The knockout mutants were obtained from the confirmed T-DNA insertion mutant collection of the Arabidopsis Biological Resource Center (ABRC): SALK_073254 (
stn7-1
) and SALK_060869 (
stn8-1
).
STN8oe
was derived from overexpression of the
STN8
coding sequence driven by a cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV) 35S promoter in the
stn8-1
mutant background. The moderate light (∼800 μmol m
−2
s
−1
) used for characterization of kinase and phosphatase mutants was provided by LED light bulbs (Feit Electric). The high light (1500 μmol m
−2
s
−1
) used to assess the stability of isolated reaction center cores was provided by a Schott KL 1600 LED light source. The far-red light used for the
in vitro
thylakoid phosphorylation assay of the wild type and
stn7stn8
was supplied by Narva 18 W/015 red fluorescent strip lamps wrapped with a layer of plasa red filter (LEE 029), which provided ∼6 μmol m
−2
s
−1
at the leaf level. 4- to 8-week-old plants were used for all experiments.
Thylakoid membranes were isolated in darkness as described previously (
McKenzie et al., 2020
) and resuspended in a small volume of ice-cold storage buffer C (0.1 M sorbitol, 50 mM HEPES, 10 mM MgCl
2
, 15 mM NaCl, pH 7.5) containing protease inhibitors (1 mg/ml Pefabloc SC, 0.3 μg/ml leupeptin, 0.2 μg/ml Antipain, and 200 μM PMSF) and 10 mM NaF. Chlorophyll concentrations of thylakoid samples were determined in 80% aqueous acetone according to the Porra method (
Porra, 2002
).
Chlorophyll fluorescence measurements
For chlorophyll fluorescence induction measurement, fresh thylakoid membranes were isolated from 6- to 8-week-old
Arabidopsis
plants. The thylakoid suspension was diluted to a final chlorophyll concentration of 10 μg/ml in storage buffer C, containing 150 mM sorbitol, and mixed with DCMU at a final concentration of 20 μM. The reaction mixture was kept on ice in complete darkness prior to each measurement. Chlorophyll fluorescence was recorded with a JTS-10 spectrophotometer (SpectroLogiX) using a custom script. In brief, thylakoid samples were excited with a weakly absorbing green LED actinic light (30 μmol m
−2
s
−1
). The detection pulses were provided by white LED light passing through a blue filter (470 nm) to preferentially excite chlorophyll a molecules. The measuring photodiode was protected with an RG665 interference filter (Schott, Mainz, Germany) and the reference diode with a BG39 filter (Schott, Mainz, Germany).
PAGE
For immunoblot analysis, thylakoid protein samples were separated on an 11.5% SDS–urea PAGE gel system. BN–PAGE analysis of thylakoid membranes was performed essentially as described previously (
Koochak et al., 2019
). In brief, freshly isolated thylakoid samples of equal chlorophyll amount were washed twice in TMK buffer (10 mM Tris–HCl [pH 6.8], 10 mM MgCl
2
, 20 mM KCl) at 5000 rpm and 4°C on a benchtop centrifuge in a total volume of 300 μl. The supernatant was discarded, and washed thylakoids were resuspended in 60 μl of ACA buffer (750 mM ε-aminocaproic acid, 50 mM imidazole [pH 7], 5 mM EDTA, 50 mM NaCl), mixed with 6 μl of freshly prepared 10% n-Dodecyl α-D-Maltoside (α-DM) to a final concentration of 0.9% α-DM, briefly vortexed, and incubated on ice for 10 min. Samples were centrifuged at 13 000 rpm for 10 min at 4°C on a benchtop centrifuge; each supernatant was mixed with 6 μl of loading buffer (750 mM ε-aminocaproic acid and 5% [w/v] pure Coomassie brilliant blue G [B0770, Sigma]) and loaded onto a 6%–12% gradient polyacrylamide gel. Gels were run at 4°C for 16 h overnight with blue cathode buffer (50 mM tricine and 7.5 mM imidazole [pH 7.0] supplemented with 0.02% Coomassie G-250) at 60 V. After the overnight run, the blue cathode buffer was exchanged with colorless cathode buffer lacking Coomassie G-250, and the gel was run at 250 V for an additional 2–4 h at 4°C. Where indicated, the intensity of the blue-native gel bands was analyzed with ImageJ. For analysis of oxidative modification, BN–PAGE gels were polymerized with 10 μM flavin mononucleotide in the presence of long-wavelength UV light to avoid artifactual oxidative protein modification from ammonium persulfate, and the gel was run with cathode buffer containing 100 mM sodium thioglycolate.
Immunoblotting
Each thylakoid sample was diluted with breaking buffer (130 mM Tris–HCl [pH 6.8], 16% [w/v] glycerol, 4.6% [w/v] SDS) and mixed with 5× Laemmli buffer, and a sample volume equivalent to 0.5 μg of chlorophyll was loaded onto an 11.5% SDS–urea PAGE gel. For 2D-PAGE, blue native gel lanes were cut out, denatured in Laemmli buffer, and embedded on the top of an SDS–urea PAGE gel with 1% molten agarose prepared in running buffer. The gel was run at 20-mA constant current for 3 h, and the proteins were transferred onto a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane at 20 V for 1 h. Upon transfer, the membrane was washed three times for 5 min each in Tris-buffered saline–Tween (0.1%), blocked in blocking buffer overnight, and incubated with primary antibody for 1 h and horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody for 1 h. Immunoreactive bands were visualized on a ChemiDoc MP imager (Bio-Rad) using a chemiluminescence detection reagent (ECL Clarity, Bio-Rad). The primary antibodies used were anti-phosphothreonine polyclonal antibody (9381, Cell Signaling), anti-D1 polyclonal antibody (AS05084, Agrisera), anti-D2 polyclonal antibody (AS06146, Agrisera), anti-CP43 polyclonal antibody (AS111787, Agrisera), anti-CP47 polyclonal antibody (AS04038, Agrisera), and anti-LHCB2 polyclonal antibody (AS01003). The secondary antibody was an anti-rabbit immunoglobulin G (AS09602, Agrisera).
For immunoblot analysis of BN–PAGE gels, gels were first incubated in a denaturing solution consisting of 1× Laemmli buffer without bromophenol blue for 30 min at room temperature, followed by Towbin buffer for 1 h at room temperature. The proteins from the gel were transferred to a PVDF membrane at 180 mA for 2 h and washed three times for 5 min each in a destaining solution (10% acetic acid, 45% MeOH) prior to blocking.
In vitro
phosphorylation of thylakoids
Six-week-old wild type and
stn7stn8
plants were moved to darkness for 16 h, followed by 2 h of far-red light illumination. Thylakoids were promptly isolated from far-red-treated plants in darkness, and chlorophyll concentration was determined. Thylakoid membranes were diluted to a chlorophyll concentration of 0.5 μg/μl in phosphorylation buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl [pH 7.5], 5 mM MgCl
2
, 1 mM MnCl
2
, and 20 mM NaF) and mixed with 25 μM ATP or buffer.
In vitro
phosphorylation was initiated by illumination of the samples with a white LED light (∼150 μmol m
−2
s
−1
) for 1 h at 21°C. Aliquots of far-red-treated diluted thylakoid samples without ATP were kept in darkness for 1 h at 21°C and used as controls. For western blot analysis, thylakoid samples equivalent to 0.5 μg of chlorophyll were immediately mixed with 5× Laemmli buffer and loaded onto an 11.5% SDS–urea PAGE gel. For blue native PAGE analysis, thylakoid samples equivalent to 50 μg of chlorophyll were withdrawn and processed for BN–PAGE as described earlier.
Exogenous ROS treatment
Thylakoid membranes equivalent to 50 μg of chlorophyll were diluted to 0.3 μg/μl chlorophyll in storage buffer C containing protease inhibitors and 10 mM NaF, then mixed with various concentrations of H
2
O
2
at 10% of the total reaction volume. Isolated PSII core complexes were treated essentially in the same manner but with an initial total chlorophyll content of 10 μg. Reactions were allowed to proceed in darkness at room temperature for 30 min or up to 1 h, depending on the experiment.
Electron transport inhibitor treatment
To test the effect of electron transport inhibitors on PSII disassembly, isolated thylakoids equivalent to 50 μg of chlorophyll were diluted to 0.3 μg/μl chlorophyll in storage buffer C and mixed with DCMU or hydroxylamine to final concentrations of 20 μM or 2 mM, respectively, at 10% of the total reaction volume. Samples were then incubated under white light (150 μmol m
−2
s
−1
) for up to 30 min and prepared for BN–PAGE.
Purification of PSII core complexes
PSII core particles were isolated as reported in
van Leeuwen et al. (1991)
, with a few minor modifications. To prepare BBY membranes,
Arabidopsis
rosettes were washed and homogenized in B1 solution (20 mM tricine [pH 7.8], 0.4 M NaCl, 2 mM MgCl
2
, 1 mM 6-aminocaproic acid, 0.2 mM benzamidine) and passed through eight layers of cheesecloth and one layer of Miracloth. Pellets were collected by centrifugation at 1400
g
and 4°C for 10 min, then resuspended in B2 solution (20 mM tricine [pH 7.8], 0.15 M NaCl, 5 mM MgCl
2
, 1 mM 6-aminocaproic acid, 0.2 mM benzamidine). The resulting membrane suspension was centrifuged at 4000
g
and 4°C for 10 min, and the pellet was resuspended in B3 solution (20 mM HEPES [pH 7.5], 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl
2
). The membranes were subsequently pelleted by centrifugation at 6000
g
and resuspended again in B3 solution to a 2-mg/ml chlorophyll concentration, and Triton X-100 was added dropwise to a final concentration of 25 mg/mg chlorophyll with slow constant stirring for 15 min. Triton-solubilized thylakoids were centrifuged at 40 000
g
for 25 min at 4°C; the pellet was resuspended in B3 solution and spun at 2000
g
for 5 min at 4°C to pellet out the starch granules. Membranes from the remaining supernatant were pelleted once again by centrifugation at 40 000
g
for 25 min at 4°C and stored in BBY storage buffer (20 mM HEPES [pH 7.5], 0.4 M sorbitol, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl
2
) containing protease inhibitors and 10 mM NaF at −80°C for further use.
BBY membranes were further washed in solution B4 (20 mM MES [pH 6], 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM CaCl
2
, 0.4 M sucrose), pelleted by centrifugation at 40 000
g
for 25 min at 4°C, and subsequently resuspended in BTS400 (20 mM Bis–Tris [pH 6.5], 20 mM MgCl
2
, 5 mM CaCl
2
, 10 mM MgSO
4
, 0.4 mM sucrose, 0.03% n-Dodecyl β-D-maltoside (β-DM). The membranes were adjusted to a 2 mg/ml chlorophyll concentration and solubilized by addition of one-seventh volume of 10% w/v β-DM to a final detergent concentration of 1.25% w/v. The membrane–detergent suspension was mixed by end-over-end inversion for 10 min, and insoluble material was pelleted at 40 000
g
for 20 min at 4°C. Solubilized membranes were applied to a Q-Sepharose FF column (Pharmacia Biotech) pre-equilibrated with BTS400. The column was washed with BTS400 until the eluate became clear, and PSII core complexes were eluted with several column volumes of BTS400 containing 75 mM MgSO
4
. Purified PSII core complexes were further concentrated with a 30-kDa Molecular Weight Cut-Off (MWCO) filter (Amicon) and desalted into storage buffer C containing protease inhibitors and 10 mM NaF.
LC–MS/MS
For oxidative modification analysis, bands corresponding to C1 and RC47 were excised from the blue native gels using a new razor, reduced in 10 mM DTT at 55°C for 1 h, and alkylated in 55 mM iodoacetamide in darkness for 45 min. In-gel digestion of proteins was performed at 37°C overnight using 2.5 μg of trypsin/Lys-C (Promega). Samples were further digested with 2.5 μg of chymotrypsin (Promega) at 25°C for 4 h. For phosphopeptide enrichment, proteins were extracted from thylakoid samples by heating at 80°C for 10 min in 40 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8), 40 mM DTT, and 4% SDS, followed by chloroform–methanol precipitation and resuspension in 8 M urea, 20 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8), and 3 mM EDTA. Protease digestion was performed essentially as above with the omission of chymotrypsin. Phosphopeptides were enriched using PolyMac beads according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Peptides were desalted with a C18 spin column according to the manufacturer’s instructions (The Nest Group). Peptides were dried and resuspended in 3% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid, peptide concentration was measured by a BCA assay (Pierce), and equal amounts of peptides were run on LC–MS/MS as described previously (
McKenzie et al., 2020
).
For oxidative modification analysis, raw files were searched using MaxQuant (1.6.14) against a custom FASTA library containing D1, D2, and CP47 proteins. Unless explicitly stated, all parameters were left in their default settings. Digestion enzymes included trypsin/P, chymotrypsin, and Lys-C, with the maximum number of missed cleavages set to two. Oxidation (M) and acetylation (N-term) were set as variable modifications, and carbamidomethylation (C) was set as a fixed modification, with the maximum number of modifications per peptide set to five. Searches for oxidative modifications were performed by addition of the respective variable modifications with specificities and monoisotopic masses derived from Unimod. Main search peptide tolerance was set to 10 ppm, minimum peptide length was set to 7, and PSM false discovery rate was set to 1%. Modified peptides were analyzed from the modificationSites text file and filtered for contaminants. Only high-confidence modifications with an amino acid localization probability of ≥0.75 and a mass error of ≤5 ppm were considered. In addition, only modifications detected in all three biological replicates were considered for this analysis. Log
2
-transformed intensity values were used to determine the significance of modifications using a two-tailed Student’s
t
-test.
For phosphoproteome analysis, phosphopeptides were searched in MaxQuant (1.6.14) against the TAIR10 protein FASTA database using trypsin/P and Lys-C as digestion enzymes with the maximum number of missed cleavages set to two. Oxidation (M), acetylation (N-term), and phosphorylation (ST) were set as variable modifications, and carbamidomethylation (C) was set as a fixed modification, with the maximum number of modifications per peptide set to five. Main search peptide tolerance was set to 10 ppm, and Peptide Spectrum Match (PSM) false discovery rate was set to 1%.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed in SigmaPlot 14.0. For comparisons of chlorophyll fluorescence induction data and F
v
/F
m
values, a one-way ANOVA was performed followed by a
post hoc
test (Holm–Sidak). For comparisons of oxidative post-translational modifications, intensity values were log
2
normalized, and a two-tailed Student’s
t
-test was performed.
